t: yapacc is an optional companion to the package manager you already have. It answers four questions that every system eventually asks, and it can make changes through your package manager without taking it over. The question The command Why is this package here? yapacc why NAME What changed since the machine last worked? yapacc timeline --since-boot What will the next upgrade do? yapacc briefing Can I take the last change back? yapacc undo It works beside pacman , apt , dnf , zypper , apk , xbps and FreeBSD's pkg . You keep using them. yapacc reads what they already record and, when you ask it to change something, runs the command they would run, after showing it to you.

New here: install it, then take the ten-minute tour . Every command in the tour is read-only. Before you let it change anything, read the gate . It is one page and it explains every prompt you will see. Looking for one command: every command lists them all, including the specialist ones that yapacc --help leaves out. Wondering whether it works on your system: what works where says what was run, on which system, and what was not. The same text ships inside the program. yapacc docs lists the built-in topics and yapacc docs --man | man -l - shows the manual page, so the documentation is there when the network is not.

These are promises about behaviour, and each one can be checked against the code. They decide what yapacc will never do. Your package manager stays yours. yapacc keeps no copy of what the native manager knows. Install or remove anything directly and yapacc is never confused by it. Nothing runs unless you ask. No daemon, timer, hook or shell alias is installed by default. Read commands change nothing , and work on a machine that has never used yapacc before. Removable without trace. Delete yapacc and everything it installed keeps working, and can be removed with native tools. Every change is gated. A plain command asks. --yes consents. --dryrun only plans. A refusal exits with code 3 and changes nothing. Changes go through your package manager , as the command it would run itself, shown in full, after its own simulation. The native log is the record; timeline and undo read it. A protection says what it does not protect against , in the output and not only in the manual. One read command talks to the outside: names sends the package name you give it to repology.org, and says so. Everything a command may contact is listed under safety and privacy .

Not a package manager. It has no repository and no package format. Not a backup. undo restores package versions. It does not restore configuration files or data; a filesystem snapshot does. Not a service. Nothing stays running and nothing contacts a server on its own. Not a configuration system. It does not manage dotfiles, services or a fleet of machines.

Program What it is Needed yapacc the command line; everything in this handbook yes yapacc-tui an interactive interface , started with yapacc i no yapacc-mcp a server for AI assistants , started with yapacc mcp no The core is one static file of under 6 MB with no shared library. When a command needs a tool the machine lacks ( curl for the news feed, sudo or doas for a change), it names the tool and exits with code 6.

yapacc is one static binary. There are three ways to get it: a release archive, a build from source, or a distribution package you build from the recipe kept beside the source. There is deliberately no curl | sh installer. A tool whose job is to show you what will happen before it happens should not start by asking you to run something you have not read.

h: Release archive (any Linux, x86_64 or aarch64)
t: Each release publishes one archive per architecture and a SHA256SUMS file. The binaries are linked statically against musl: they need no shared library and run on any Linux distribution. Unpack it into a prefix. System-wide: Or for yourself only, without root: Make sure ~/.local/bin is on your PATH in that case. Then:

Path under the prefix What bin/yapacc the command line lib/yapacc/yapacc-tui the optional interactive interface ( yapacc i ) lib/yapacc/yapacc-mcp the optional server for AI assistants ( yapacc mcp ) share/man/man1/yapacc.1 the manual page share/bash-completion/ , share/zsh/ , share/fish/ shell completions LICENSE , README.md the licence and the readme Only bin/yapacc is required. Delete the other two binaries if you do not want them; yapacc doctor then reports them as optional components that are not installed.

h: Checking where the archive was built
t: The release workflow attaches a build provenance attestation to every archive. With the GitHub command line tool: The checksum proves the file is the one that was published. The attestation proves which workflow run, from which commit, built it.
You need Rust 1.89 or newer and a C linker. That builds the three binaries. For the core alone, which is all the commands in this handbook need: For a static binary you can copy to another machine:
Build on FreeBSD itself, with the Rust from packages: This was done on FreeBSD 15.1 and takes about two minutes. There is no pre-built FreeBSD binary.

Feature Default What it adds tui on builds yapacc-tui alpm off links libalpm on Arch for transaction analysis; see the note below The alpm feature uses a Rust crate published under GPL-3.0, while yapacc is GPL-2.0-only. It is there for local builds on Arch. No release archive or packaging recipe enables it, and everything in this handbook works without it.

Recipes for five distributions live in contrib/packaging . They are not in any distribution's repository yet; you build the package yourself and install it with your package manager, which then owns the files. Distribution Recipe Build Arch Linux arch/PKGBUILD makepkg -si Debian, Ubuntu debian/ dpkg-buildpackage -us -uc -b Fedora and relatives rpm/yapacc.spec rpmbuild -ba Alpine Linux alpine/APKBUILD abuild -r Void Linux void/template ./xbps-src pkg yapacc The packaging README has the details for each, including which Rust version the distribution needs.

Nothing has to be configured. yapacc works with no configuration file, and the read commands need no setup at all. Start with the quick start . Shell completions are installed by the archive and the packages. For a source build:

yapacc installs no service, no hook and no timer, so removing it is removing its files. Archive: delete bin/yapacc , lib/yapacc/ , the manual page and the three completion files from the prefix you unpacked into. Package: remove it with your package manager. Files yapacc may have created under your home directory, all safe to delete: Path What ~/.config/yapacc/ your configuration file, if you wrote one; yapacc never writes it ~/.cache/yapacc/ build caches, and downloads of an undo while it runs ~/.local/state/yapacc/ the ledger of installs made outside the package manager ~/.local/share/yapacc/ AppImages, recipes and isolated installs, if you used those commands Native packages installed or upgraded through yapacc belong to your package manager and are not affected.
Every command on this page is read-only. None of them writes a file, needs root or changes a package, so you can run them on a machine you care about.

doctor prints one line per check. It is the first thing to run on a new machine, and the first thing to attach to a bug report. warn means something a feature of this system uses is missing, and the line says what you lose. fail means a command will not work, and the line says why. n/a means the check does not apply here, or an optional part is not installed. A healthy machine shows ok and n/a only. More about doctor .
Pick a package you do not remember installing. The because line is the chain from this package back to something you asked for. More about why .
When something broke after a reboot, yapacc timeline --since-boot shows only what changed since the machine last started. More about timeline .

h: 4. Ask what the next upgrade will do
t: briefing reads the list of pending updates as of your last repository refresh. It does not refresh on its own. More about briefing .

h: 5. See what an undo would do, without doing it
t: --dryrun plans and never applies. On undo it shows the last transaction, the reverse of it, and the native manager's own simulation. A dry run writes nothing. When an old version is in no local cache, the plan says which archive it would come from, and the download happens only after you have agreed. More about undo .
None of the three changes anything. Each prints the command you would run yourself. More about them .
To let yapacc make a change, read the gate first, then install, remove, upgrade . For scripts, JSON output and exit codes . The same documentation offline: yapacc docs .

yapacc why NAME says why a package is installed, what still needs it, where it came from and how it was verified. It is read-only, and it answers for any package, whether or not yapacc had anything to do with installing it.

Line What it tells you what the package's own one-line description why the reason it is installed; the wordings are listed below because the chain back to a package you installed yourself; several lines when several of your packages lead to it needed by the installed packages that depend on it directly from the repository it came from installed when it was last installed or upgraded verified how the package manager checked it packager who built the package, as the package records it ledger whether yapacc itself has a record of installing it The why line is one of these: It says Meaning you (or a tool acting for you) installed it explicitly the package manager has it marked as asked for pulled in as a dependency something you installed needs it; because shows the chain part of the base system the package manager protects it ( Essential on apt), or the distribution gives it priority required installed as a dependency, but nothing needs it any more (orphan) yapacc inspect orphans lists it, and yapacc remove orphans would remove it installed as a dependency; nothing depends on it, but apt keeps it another package recommends or suggests it, so apt-get autoremove leaves it alone manager does not record an install reason here the package manager has no such record for this package The from line is never left empty. When the manager cannot say, the line says that: on apt, a package whose installed version has since been replaced in the index reads "the installed version is no longer in the repository index (a newer one is, from …)"; on zypper the line names the repository that offers the package now, because the zypp history does not record where the installed version came from. When part of the answer could not be checked, the line starts with note: and says what was missing. yapacc does not guess. Not every package manager records every fact, and a line that has no source is left out: apk records no install date, and FreeBSD's pkg has no verified line. On a long needed by list the terminal shows the first few names and a count. --json lists all of them.

why prints one block for each place that knows the name: the native package, a flatpak with a matching name, and anything yapacc installed itself outside the package manager (an AppImage, for example).
Code Meaning 0 found, answer printed 2 the name is not a valid package name 4 not installed anywhere yapacc can see

reason is explicit , dependency or unknown . orphan is true or false as the package manager's own orphan list says, null when that was not asked or is not known, and native.base is "essential" , "priority required" or empty. --json goes before the command. See scripting .

yapacc inspect owns /usr/bin/env finds the package that owns a file. yapacc inspect files NAME lists the files of a package. yapacc inspect orphans lists dependencies nothing needs any more; yapacc clean reports how much space they take.

yapacc timeline lists package installs, upgrades and removals, newest first, from the logs your package manager already keeps. It is read-only and it keeps no log of its own. Each line is the time, the log it came from, what happened ( install , upgrade , downgrade , reinstall , remove ), the package and the version: old and new for an upgrade or a downgrade. dpkg's log calls every version change an upgrade; yapacc compares the two versions as dpkg does and says which it was. The downgrades above are an undo : it is a transaction like any other.

h: What changed since it last worked?
t: --since-boot starts at the boot before the current one, because the question is usually "it worked yesterday, then I rebooted". The first line says which moment was used and where it came from, and a ── boot ── line marks where the machine restarted: what is listed below it was changed before the reboot. When only the current boot is known, a note says so and the list starts there instead. The boot time comes from journalctl --list-boots where there is a journal, otherwise from the kernel ( /proc/stat on Linux, sysctl kern.boottime on FreeBSD).

Option Effect --since YYYY-MM-DD only changes on or after that day (UTC) --since-boot only changes since the previous boot --limit N at most N changes; the default is 50 --html write one self-contained HTML page to standard output --html is meant for bug reports: yapacc timeline --html > timeline.html gives a single file with no external reference. It cannot be combined with --json .

Package manager Log read pacman /var/log/pacman.log apt /var/log/dpkg.log , including rotated and compressed files dnf dnf's own history database ( dnf history ) zypper /var/log/zypp/history , including rotated and compressed files apk /var/log/apk.log , when it exists pkg (FreeBSD) /var/log/messages xbps none: xbps keeps no log, and timeline says so Some of these logs are readable by root only (openSUSE's /var/log/zypp is one). timeline then says which file exists and may not be read, tells you to run sudo yapacc timeline , and exits with code 6. yapacc platform marks such a log (exists; not readable by this user) . Times are printed as the log wrote them. A log that records local time without a zone (apt, zypper) is labelled (local) . With --since-boot such a time is compared with the boot instant as if it were UTC, so a change made within your zone offset of the reboot can land on the wrong side of it; a note says so whenever it applies. A log can be silent about a run. apk run with --quiet records that it ran and not what it did, and timeline then says how many runs it could not describe ("3 apk run(s) were logged without package details") instead of leaving them out without a word.
ts is seconds since the Unix epoch. action is install , upgrade , downgrade , reinstall or remove ; a reinstall has an empty old_version .
yapacc briefing tells you what the next upgrade will do before you run it. It is read-only: it reads the list of pending updates and reports what deserves attention.

Needs attention sorts the pending packages by what they mean for you: Label Meaning reboot a kernel, C library or init system update: the new code runs only after a reboot. Kernels are recognised under the names each system gives them ( linux-image-… , kernel-default , linux6.12 , linux-lts , FreeBSD's FreeBSD-kernel-… ) care the package manager itself, the boot loader or remote access is being updated: do not interrupt, and keep a second session open over ssh info major version changes, worth a look at the release notes Security fixes lists the pending updates that fix known vulnerabilities, where the system has a source for that: the security repository on Debian and Ubuntu (an update that several repositories offer counts when one of them is the security one), the advisory data of dnf and zypper, and arch-audit on Arch when it is installed. Where there is no source, a note says so instead of printing an empty list. Distribution news shows recent announcements from the distribution's feed. Lines marked ! announce a manual step. This is the one part of briefing that uses the network (through curl ); --offline skips it. Distributions without a machine-readable feed get a note saying so, as Debian does above. On Arch, which has one: Configuration files still unmerged lists what earlier upgrades left for you to merge. yapacc configs shows how to compare each one. Disk shows free space where packages are written. Safety net says whether a snapshot tool is available and reminds you what undo does and does not restore.

briefing reads the pending list as of your last repository refresh ( apt-get update , pacman -Sy , dnf makecache and so on) and says so in a note. A read command never refreshes repositories for you, and never lets the package manager do it behind your back: on dnf and zypper, where the native tool would fetch metadata on its own, yapacc asks it for cached data only. If the list looks old, refresh with your package manager, or run yapacc refresh , which is gated like any other change. On a machine that has never refreshed (a fresh image, a new container) there is no pending list to read. yapacc says that, and names the command, instead of reporting that nothing is pending: briefing then opens with "pending packages not known" and the same note. On Arch, when checkupdates is installed but fails, the briefing says the list below it is not current and why.
Option Effect --offline do not fetch the distribution's news feed
yapacc upgrade runs the full upgrade through the native manager, with the plan and the gate. See install, remove, upgrade .

yapacc undo takes the last package transaction back. It reads the last transaction from the native log, works out its reverse, shows you the plan and the exact command, and asks before doing anything. On apt the plan includes apt's own simulation of the reverse; on dnf it is dnf's own description of the transaction. It works on pacman, apt, dnf and zypper. On apk, xbps and FreeBSD's pkg it says that undo is not available there. That is the plan for taking back an upgrade of two packages on Debian 13. A whole system upgrade is undone the same way. This one was a yapacc upgrade of 24 packages and a new kernel, taken back for real on a virtual machine: The last line is a check. When the native command has returned, yapacc reads the installed versions again and compares them with the plan.

The transaction did this Undo does this installed a package removes it removed a package installs that version again upgraded a package restores the previous version downgraded a package restores the newer version Undo acts on one transaction: the most recent one in the native log. An undo is itself a transaction, and timeline shows it like any other. Undo restores package versions . It does not restore configuration files, databases or anything a package script changed. Only a filesystem snapshot does that; see snapshots . The output repeats this every time.

To restore a previous version, yapacc has to find that exact version. It looks in this order and tells you, per package, where it found it: Package manager Sources, in order Verification pacman the pacman cache, then the Arch Linux Archive the archive's detached signature, verified with pacman-key before the package is installed apt on Debian the configured repositories, the apt cache, then snapshot.debian.org repositories: apt's own; snapshot.debian.org: checked against the recorded hash, not signature-verified apt on Ubuntu the configured repositories, the apt cache, then Launchpad repositories: apt's own; Launchpad downloads are not verified, and the output says so dnf the enabled repositories, through dnf's own history undo dnf's own zypper the configured repositories only zypper's own All or nothing. If one old version cannot be found anywhere, the whole undo is refused (exit code 3) and nothing is changed. yapacc does not apply half of an undo. On dnf, the old versions are checked for availability before the gate, so a refusal comes from the dry run and not from the middle of the real one. On zypper there is no archive to fall back on: on a rolling distribution such as Tumbleweed, the repositories drop old versions quickly, and an undo of an upgrade more than a day or two old is usually refused for that reason. A dry run downloads nothing: it asks the archive whether the file exists and reports where each version would come from, with its size when the archive gives one. The real run downloads after you have agreed, into a private directory under ~/.cache/yapacc/undo that is deleted when the undo ends. On apt, when files have to be downloaded, you are asked twice: once before the download, and once more with apt's simulation of the restore in front of you. --yes answers both. An archive that does not answer is not an archive that lacks the version. A lookup waits 20 seconds for the connection and 60 in all, and is tried twice. If there is still no answer the undo is refused (exit code 3) with "did not answer … so it is not known whether it has that version", and you try again later. Only an archive that answered "no" produces "is in no local cache and no configured repository, and the archive of this distribution … does not have it". On zypper the same care applies to the repositories: without repository metadata on disk, yapacc cannot know whether a repository still has the old version, says so, and refuses. zypper refresh first.

The last lines say What happened Verified: N of N package(s) are at the planned state. the undo is complete The package versions were restored (N of N verified), but apt reported an error … every version is back, and the native manager still ended with an error, often a package script that failed. Read its output above; exit code 1 K of N package(s) are not at the planned state: … the native command failed part of the way, or reported success and left a difference. The packages are named; yapacc timeline shows the current state; exit code 1

Undo refuses rather than doing something it cannot stand behind. The running kernel. An undo that would remove the kernel the machine is running on is refused until you have rebooted into another kernel. Packages that something else needs. If removing a package would break a package installed since, the native manager's dependency check refuses it and yapacc stops. Failed verification. A file from the Arch Linux Archive without a signature that verifies, or a file from snapshot.debian.org whose hash does not match, is deleted and the undo stops with exit code 5. More than was planned. On apt, if the simulation shows that the undo would also remove a package that was not part of the transaction, the undo is refused. Unknown history on zypper. libzypp records an upgrade as an install of the new version, so for a package with no earlier record yapacc cannot tell "new dependency" from "upgraded". When undoing a whole zypper up or dup , it names those packages and asks at the terminal whether to remove them. --yes , --script and a pipe do not answer that question: without a terminal the undo is refused.

Reading the last transaction may itself need root: openSUSE keeps /var/log/zypp/history readable by root only, so there you run sudo yapacc undo . Elsewhere, run it as yourself; yapacc calls sudo or doas for the one command that changes the system.

Option Effect --dryrun show the last transaction and the plan; download and apply nothing --yes apply without the [y/N] question Without either, undo shows the plan and asks. See the gate . With [safety] snapshot set, a snapshot is taken after you consent and before the first package is touched, as for any other change. On dnf the plan names the transaction by its ID, and that ID is what is undone, even if another transaction has been committed since you read the plan. On Debian and Ubuntu, multiarch packages are shown and handled with their architecture ( libfoo:i386 ).

One transaction, the last one. There is no "undo the last three" and no undo of a transaction further back. A restored package is upgraded again by the next full upgrade unless you hold it yourself ( IgnorePkg in pacman.conf, apt-mark hold , a dnf or zypper lock). Undoing an install removes the package and does not purge it. On apt its configuration files stay, as after any apt-get remove (state rc in dpkg -l ). apt does not remove a package it counts as essential under -y , and yapacc does not override that, with one exception: packages of a foreign architecture that the transaction itself installed. An undo that would need more is refused, and the message says which package. No undo on apk, xbps or pkg. It has been run end to end on booted virtual machines of Arch, Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04, Fedora 45, Rocky Linux 9.9, openSUSE Leap 16.1 and Tumbleweed, including kernel upgrades followed by a real reboot. It has not been run on real hardware. What works where has the detail.
Three reports for the day after an upgrade. All three are read-only: each prints what it found and the command you would run yourself, and none of them runs it for you.

yapacc clean measures what can be reclaimed. It looks at: packages installed as dependencies that nothing needs any more (orphans); the package manager's download cache; yapacc's own cache; unused runtimes of other sources, such as flatpak, when they are present. Each item is labelled [safe] or [review] . safe means removing it loses nothing that cannot be fetched again, and the line says what the cost is. review means read the list first: an orphan may be something you use directly. When part of a cache cannot be read without root, the size is a lower bound and the output says so. Only package files are counted: a cache directory that holds nothing but a lock file or an index is not listed. On dnf the cache is reported as two items with two commands, because they are two different decisions: the downloaded packages ( sudo dnf clean packages ) and the repository metadata ( sudo dnf clean metadata ), which dnf fetches again on its next run. On Fedora a third item can appear: the copy of the repository metadata dnf5 keeps for each ordinary user in ~/.cache/libdnf5 . It is labelled safe , and dnf makes the copy again the next time that user asks it about the repositories. Orphans come from the package manager's own answer. On a machine with no repository metadata on disk, dnf and zypper cannot give that answer; clean then says "orphans are not known" and why, and reports the rest. To remove orphans through yapacc, with the list shown and a question asked: yapacc remove orphans . See install, remove, upgrade .

yapacc restart says what still runs old code after an upgrade. That is a Debian 13 machine just after an upgrade that brought a new kernel and new OpenSSL, zlib and PCRE libraries. Each service comes with the command to restart it, and with a caution where restarting it would hurt (the message bus, the login manager). After the reboot it asks for, the same command has nothing left to say: Reboot is yes , no or unknown , with the reason. It uses what the system offers: the distribution's own reboot flag ( /run/reboot-required , /run/reboot-needed ), needs-restarting -r on dnf systems, a comparison of the running kernel with the installed ones, and freebsd-version on FreeBSD. unknown means none of these could answer, and the line says why. Services and programs are processes that still map a file an upgrade replaced. On systemd, processes are matched to their service. On other init systems the programs are listed and the output tells you how to restart a service there. An ordinary user cannot read every process. restart then says how many it could not examine ("Not examined: 16 process(es) that this user may not read") and to run it as root for the whole picture: on the machine above, before the reboot, the same command without sudo found the kernel and none of the nine services. The Limits line at the end states what this method cannot see at all.

yapacc configs lists configuration files that an upgrade left for you to merge: .pacnew and .pacsave on Arch; .dpkg-dist , .dpkg-old , .dpkg-new and .ucf-dist on Debian and Ubuntu; .rpmnew and .rpmsave on Fedora and openSUSE; .apk-new on Alpine. For each file it says which file it belongs to, which of the two is yours, when each was written, and the command to compare them. A saved file whose live file is gone (a .pacsave or .rpmsave left by a removed package) is described as that: "your old file, saved; the live file no longer exists". It merges nothing. Directories under /etc that an ordinary user cannot read are counted and reported, so you know when to run it again as root. yapacc briefing shows the same list in short form, because unmerged configuration is worth settling before the next upgrade adds to it.
Two read-only commands that describe the machine. Run doctor first on any new system, and attach both to a bug report.

yapacc doctor prints one line per check: what works on this machine, what does not, and why. State Meaning ok it works warn something a feature of this system uses is missing or weaker; the line says what you lose fail a command will not work until this is fixed; the line says why n/a the check does not apply to this system, or an optional part ( yapacc-tui , yapacc-mcp , flatpak, gpgv) is not installed; the line says what it would be for A healthy machine shows ok and n/a only, as above. The lines for undo , timeline and briefing say what each can do on this machine : where old versions would come from, which log is read, whether there is a news feed. A system without a package log gets "no timeline" here, not an empty timeline later. yapacc --json doctor gives the same list as an array of {name, state, detail} .

yapacc platform says what kind of machine this is, one line per axis. Each axis is detected on its own; yapacc does not assume that a distribution implies an init system or a boot loader. Where an axis could only be read in part, the line says so, as for the boot loader above. A package log that is there but closed to you is marked (exists; not readable by this user) . When a machine has several package managers installed, the native one is the one whose database owns /usr/lib/os-release . dnf and zypper read the same rpm database; between them it is the one that has repositories configured, and zypper on SUSE, dnf elsewhere, when both have. The other one is listed on an other managers line. The last line is the support tier of the native package manager. What works where explains the tiers.
Every command that changes the system goes through the same gate. This page describes it once; it applies to install , remove , upgrade , refresh , undo and snapshot create on every package manager.

Plan. yapacc prints what will be installed, removed, upgraded or restored. A request that cannot be right stops here: removing a package that is not installed is "not found" (exit code 4) before anything is simulated. Simulation. It runs the native manager's own dry run of that plan and prints the result as the manager says it. If the simulation fails, the change is refused (exit code 3) and you are not asked. Command. It prints the exact command it is about to run. Gate. It asks, unless you have already answered with a flag. Apply. It runs the command, through sudo or doas when you are not root. Your yes is the only question: the native manager is told not to ask again ( apt-get -y , pacman --noconfirm , dnf -y ), and the plan shows the command with those flags. Record. The native manager writes its log as usual. yapacc keeps no second record of native changes. Closing line. yapacc says what the run amounted to, from the installed packages and not from the exit status alone: Done , or "Nothing was changed: apt had nothing to do (the installed packages are the same as before)", or, after a failure, whether packages were changed before it failed. Answer anything but yes and nothing happens:

You run What happens the plain command the plan is shown and you are asked [y/N] ; Enter means no with --yes the plan is shown and applied without a question with --dryrun the plan and the simulation are shown; nothing is applied with --script never prompts; needs --yes or --dryrun , otherwise it is a refusal with input from a pipe cannot answer the question, so it is a refusal unless --yes or --dryrun is given --noconfirm is accepted as another spelling of --yes . The question follows your locale: [o/N] in French, [j/N] in German. English y and yes are always accepted.

When the answer is no, or nobody could be asked, the command exits with code 3 and has changed nothing. The message says which of the two it was: Code 3 is only ever a refusal. A change that was attempted and failed exits 1. See exit codes .

h: A few questions --yes does not answer
t: --yes consents to the plan you could have read. It does not consent to things that need your eyes or that yapacc cannot know. In those cases it asks at the terminal and, when there is no terminal, refuses: packages with no earlier record when undoing a whole upgrade on zypper ( undo ); the review of a build recipe (a PKGBUILD from the AUR) before it is built; --no-review is the explicit way to skip it; a non-free licence on a package installed from outside the repositories; --non-free accepts it in advance. --yes and --dryrun together are a usage error (exit code 2).

Run yapacc as yourself. For the one command that needs root it uses sudo , or doas where that is what the machine has, and the password prompt you see is theirs. With --script , or when there is no terminal, the tool is called in its non-interactive mode ( sudo -n , doas -n ). If it would need a password, the command fails at once instead of waiting for input nobody can give. dnf and zypper need root even to simulate. At a terminal the simulation runs through sudo or doas , so the password prompt can come before the plan. In a run that may not ask ( --script , no terminal) it runs behind sudo -n or doas -n when that lets you through; when it does not, the plan says "no simulation" and why. As root, no tool is used. When neither sudo nor doas is present and you are not root, the plan is still shown, and the command exits with code 6 naming what is missing.

When [safety] snapshot is set to auto or auto-best-effort in the configuration , yapacc takes a filesystem snapshot after you consent and before the native command runs. The plan says so, and the question becomes "Proceed (a snapper snapshot is taken first)". A dry run takes no snapshot. When no snapshot can be taken, the plan says that too, before you answer. See snapshots .
It is not a sandbox. Once you answer yes, the native manager runs with the privileges it always has, and package scripts do what package scripts do. The gate makes sure you saw the plan first.

yapacc can make the common changes through your package manager. It adds three things to running the native command yourself: the plan and the native simulation are always shown first, the gate is the same on every system, and a snapshot can be taken before the change. You never have to use these commands. Changes you make directly with apt , pacman or dnf are just as visible to timeline and undo .

Command What it does yapacc install repo PKG… install packages from the distribution's repositories yapacc remove repo PKG… remove packages yapacc remove orphans remove dependencies that nothing needs any more yapacc upgrade full system upgrade yapacc refresh refresh the repository indexes only yapacc get NAME choose a source for NAME, then install it All of them take --dryrun and --yes , and all of them stop at the gate without one of the two. A full upgrade reads the same way. This is the machine of the quick start , two months behind:

yapacc builds no shell command. Package names are validated, then passed as separate arguments after -- , so a name can never be read as an option. This is the command behind each verb: Manager install remove upgrade refresh pacman pacman -S pacman -Rs pacman -Syu pacman -Sy apt apt-get install -y apt-get remove -y apt-get update , then apt-get upgrade --with-new-pkgs -y apt-get update dnf dnf install -y dnf remove -y dnf upgrade --refresh -y dnf makecache --refresh zypper zypper install zypper remove zypper dist-upgrade on rolling releases, zypper update otherwise zypper refresh apk apk add apk del apk update , then apk upgrade apk update xbps xbps-install -y xbps-remove -y xbps-install -Syu xbps-install -S pkg pkg install -y pkg delete -y pkg upgrade -y pkg update The simulation shown before the gate is the same manager's dry run of the same request ( apt-get -s , dnf --assumeno , zypper --dry-run , apk --simulate , xbps-install -n , pkg -n , pacman --print ). If the simulation itself fails, the change is refused (exit code 3) before you are asked anything: an unknown name or a broken dependency stops there. Two simulations cannot be judged by their status: dnf's --assumeno always ends with an error status, and so does pkg install -n whenever there is something to install. yapacc reads what they print instead. When dnf says it could not resolve the request (an unknown name, a conflict, a protected package), an install or a removal is refused in the same way, with exit code 3. An upgrade is the one change a failed simulation does not refuse, on dnf and on pacman: the simulation runs without the refresh the real command begins with, so its failure says little. A note says that the simulation failed, and you are still asked. A removal of something that is not installed never gets that far. It is "not found" (exit code 4) on every package manager. A name that an installed package provides, and a pacman group with installed members, are not refused. On FreeBSD yapacc asks the catalogue on disk first and refuses a name that is not in it (exit code 4), with the hint to run pkg update . A name pkg itself answers "No packages available to install matching" for is refused with the same code. With no catalogue on disk, pkg install -n prints nothing; a note under the simulation heading then says that there is no repository metadata and names pkg update . On Arch, before the repository databases were ever fetched, install repo is refused with exit code 6: nothing can be planned from no database. The message names pacman -Syu and yapacc upgrade , which runs it behind the gate. A removal on pacman is -Rs : the package and the dependencies nothing else needs. Configuration files you modified are kept as .pacsave . pacman is always run with --noconfirm : you answered at the gate, and pacman does not ask a second time.

It says What happened Done. the packages changed as planned Nothing was changed: apt had nothing to do … the command ran without error and the installed packages are the same as before No package was changed: … refreshed its repository indexes and had nothing to upgrade an upgrade with nothing pending Nothing was changed: the installed packages are the same as before. the command failed before touching a package Packages were changed before it failed: `yapacc timeline` shows what was changed. the command failed part of the way yapacc works this out by comparing the installed packages before and after, so the line is true even when the native manager's exit status is not informative. On apt, upgrade uses --with-new-pkgs , so kernel upgrades that need a new package are included. It does not remove packages; use your package manager's full-upgrade when a release change requires that.

Run yapacc briefing first. It tells you whether the upgrade touches the kernel, the C library, the package manager or ssh, and shows the distribution's announcements. After it, yapacc restart says what still runs old code and whether a reboot is due, and yapacc configs lists configuration files the upgrade left for you to merge. If the upgrade went wrong, yapacc undo takes it back.

yapacc get NAME looks for NAME in the sources this machine has and installs from the first that has it. The distribution's own package comes first. --explain shows the decision and stops. Off Arch, get knows the distribution's repositories and flatpak; it shows a flatpak match and does not install it for you. On Arch it also knows the AUR and local recipes, and takes the first source in the order repo, aur, flatpak, recipe that has the name; [install] order in the configuration changes that order, and --from repo|aur|flatpak|recipe forces one source for one run.

The commands above cover the native package manager, which is what most people need. yapacc also has specialist commands for other sources: flatpak, AppImages, the AUR on Arch with a review step and a sandboxed build, and isolated installs of packages made for another distribution. yapacc --help does not list them; every command does.

undo restores package versions. A filesystem snapshot restores everything else: configuration files, data that package scripts rewrote, and the packages too. yapacc does not implement snapshots. It drives the snapshot tool the machine already has.

Tool List Create Notes snapper yes yes the usual tool on openSUSE; works on any btrfs layout snapper is configured for timeshift yes yes rsync mode and btrfs mode zfs yes yes snapshots the dataset of the root filesystem plain btrfs yes no subvolumes are listed; yapacc does not create plain btrfs snapshots yapacc platform shows which of these it detected, on the snapshots line.

snapshot create is a change, so it goes through the gate : --dryrun shows the command, --yes skips the question, and yapacc calls sudo or doas as it does for any change. snapshot list is a read command and elevates nothing: where the tool only answers root, it says so (exit code 6), and you run sudo yapacc snapshot list . On a machine without a snapshot tool, both say what was looked for:

Set this in the configuration and yapacc takes a snapshot before install , remove and upgrade , after you have consented and before the native command runs. Value When a tool is found When the snapshot fails off nothing n/a auto a snapshot is taken first the change is refused (exit code 3) auto-best-effort a snapshot is taken first a warning is printed and the change goes on The plan names the tool and the command before you are asked, and a dry run never takes a snapshot; it only says one would be taken.

h: When no snapshot can be taken
t: The plan tells you before the question, and a dry run tells you the same: Situation auto auto-best-effort snapshot_provider = "auto" and the machine has no snapshot tool the change runs without a snapshot; the plan says "No snapshot will be taken: … there is no snapshot tool on this machine" the same a named provider that cannot work here refused (exit code 3), with the reason and the three ways out a warning in the plan; the change runs without a snapshot the snapshot command fails refused (exit code 3); nothing was changed a warning; the change goes on The reason for a named provider is one of: the tool is not installed, snapper has no root config ( snapper -c root create-config / sets one up), / is not on ZFS, or the provider is plain btrfs, which yapacc lists and does not create. The first row is deliberate. auto for the provider means "use what is there", and on a machine with nothing there, refusing every change would make the setting unusable in a configuration shared between machines. If you want a change refused whenever no snapshot is possible, name the provider. If timeshift was never set up, its first --create picks a snapshot device on its own and writes its configuration. Set timeshift up yourself before letting anything call it. yapacc prints this warning in the plan when it applies.

yapacc creates and lists snapshots. It does not restore them. Rolling a root filesystem back is done with the snapshot tool itself, often from a rescue or boot environment: snapper: snapper rollback , or boot a snapshot from the boot menu on openSUSE; timeshift: timeshift --restore ; zfs: zfs rollback , or boot environments with bectl on FreeBSD. This is deliberate. A rollback of the running root is the kind of operation where a companion tool should step aside.

Creating and listing were run against the real tools on virtual machines: snapper on openSUSE Leap 16.1 and Tumbleweed and on Arch, timeshift 24.06 in rsync mode on Debian 13 and 26.11 in btrfs mode on Arch, and zfs on FreeBSD 14.5 and 15.1 with a ZFS root. Not verified: a restore of any kind (yapacc does not do one), and snapper on a distribution other than those three.

This page says what yapacc does on each package manager, and how that was checked. The run-by-run evidence is in the verification log ; the current state of the project is in STATUS.md . On your own machine, yapacc doctor is the authority: it reports what works there .
why , list , info , search , check , inspect , clean , doctor and platform work on all seven package managers. The gated install , remove and upgrade do too. The differences are in the rest.

Manager It ran on timeline briefing adds restart configs pacman Arch yes distribution news; security with arch-audit yes yes apt Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04 yes security, kernel yes yes dnf Fedora 45, Rocky 9.9 yes security yes yes zypper openSUSE Leap 16.1, Tumbleweed yes, as root security yes yes apk Alpine 3.24 yes, when apk keeps a log pending and reboot only yes yes xbps Void no: xbps keeps no log pending and reboot only yes no pkg FreeBSD 14.5, 15.1 yes pending and reboot only kernel; processes with checkrestart no

Every system in the first row was a booted virtual machine built from the distribution's public cloud image (Void: an image built from the official container), with an ordinary user going through sudo or doas , and as root. The commands were run for real: packages installed, upgraded, removed and restored, prompts answered at a terminal, machines rebooted into old and new kernels. On top of that, one static binary is run in containers of seven distributions by the test suite, and the parsers are tested against output captured from the real tools. What that does not cover: Real hardware. Every run was a virtual machine or a container. Other architectures. Everything ran on x86_64. The aarch64 archive is built, and its binaries were started under emulation; nothing more was run on that architecture. Derivatives. Linux Mint, Pop! _ OS, Manjaro, EndeavourOS, AlmaLinux, RHEL and SLES were not run. They use the same package managers, so the commands are expected to work, and yapacc doctor will tell you; undo 's archive fallback knows Debian, Ubuntu and Arch only. Other users. Until this release nobody but the author had used it.

yapacc platform prints a support tier for the native package manager. Tier Managers Meaning 1 pacman, apt, dnf the main targets: everything in the table, including undo 2 zypper, apk, xbps, pkg read commands and gated changes work; some features are missing, as the table shows 3 portage, nix detected only; changes are refused, with the reason

OpenBSD and NetBSD. There is no backend for pkg_add or pkgin . Portage and Nix. yapacc recognises the system and refuses to change it, saying why. Read commands have no backend there. Image-based systems (ostree, such as Fedora Silverblue or openSUSE MicroOS). They are detected and nothing more: package changes on those systems are not what yapacc's gate models.

undo restores package versions, not configuration or data, and it is all or nothing: when one old version cannot be found the whole undo is refused. zypper and dnf have no archive to fall back on. Once a repository drops an old version, an upgrade that replaced it cannot be undone. On Tumbleweed that is a day or two. Old packages from snapshot.debian.org are checked against the recorded hash and not signature-verified. Launchpad downloads are not verified. The output says which applies. Snapshots are taken through snapper, timeshift or zfs. Plain btrfs is listed only. yapacc never restores a snapshot. The sandbox for third-party builds has no seccomp filter and no resource limits. restart cannot see interpreters holding replaced scripts, statically linked programs, or kernel live patches, and it says so every time. STATUS.md carries the full list.
What is specific to each system: which commands yapacc runs, where the history comes from, and the things worth knowing before you rely on it.

Changes run pacman -S , pacman -Rs and pacman -Syu , always with --noconfirm : you answer once, at yapacc's gate, with pacman's plan in front of you. yapacc never runs pacman -Sy followed by an install: a partial upgrade is the usual way to break an Arch system. yapacc refresh exists and prints that warning. Timeline reads /var/log/pacman.log . Undo looks in /var/cache/pacman/pkg first, then downloads from the Arch Linux Archive with the package's signature; a package whose signature is missing or does not verify stops the undo. A restored package is upgraded again by the next pacman -Syu unless you add it to IgnorePkg . Briefing shows the Arch news feed, which is where manual interventions are announced. Security labels need arch-audit . The pending list comes from checkupdates (pacman-contrib) when it is installed, which does not touch the system's sync database; when it is installed and fails, the briefing says the list is not current and why. Before the first pacman -Syu (a fresh image, a new container) there is no sync database. list then cannot tell which packages are foreign and says so instead of calling all of them foreign. check and search say "no repository metadata on disk" and name pacman -Syu ; check does not ask the AUR in that state, because it cannot tell which installed packages come from there and would send every name. install repo is refused with exit code 6 and the same advice. Network: on Arch, check asks the AUR about packages that are not in the repositories, and get asks it about the name you give. See safety and privacy . libalpm. The release binaries talk to pacman through its command and are not linked against libalpm. A few specialist commands ( install alpm , inspect alpm … ) exist only in a build made with the alpm feature; in any other build they exit with code 6 and name the command that does the same through pacman. The AUR is available through specialist commands ( yapacc install aur NAME ): the PKGBUILD is shown for review before anything is built, and the build runs in a bubblewrap sandbox. The name is looked up first: one that is not in the AUR is "not found" (exit code 4) before anything is cloned, and when aur.archlinux.org cannot be reached the command stops with exit code 6. aur pkgbuild NAME needs only curl . See every command .

Changes run apt-get install , apt-get remove , and for an upgrade apt-get update then apt-get upgrade --with-new-pkgs . That installs new kernels and never removes a package; a release upgrade that needs removals is still apt full-upgrade , by hand. Timeline reads /var/log/dpkg.log and its rotated, compressed predecessors. dpkg logs local time without a zone, so entries are labelled (local) . A fresh cloud image has no dpkg.log until the first change; doctor says so. Undo tries the configured repositories, then /var/cache/apt/archives , then the distribution's archive: snapshot.debian.org on Debian (the file is checked against the hash the service records) and Launchpad on Ubuntu (not verified, and the output says so). It refuses to remove the kernel the machine is running. Multiarch names are kept as they are: libfoo:i386 stays libfoo:i386 through undo , and why answers for a package of a foreign architecture with its own reason and origin. Three gaps remain: why libfoo:i386 is refused as a name (ask for libfoo ), list shows a package installed for two architectures as two rows that look alike, and timeline drops the architecture suffix. Briefing marks updates that come from the security repository ( -security on both; on Ubuntu an update offered by -security and -updates at once counts). There is no machine-readable news feed for Debian or Ubuntu, and the briefing says so. Why tells an orphan from a dependency that apt keeps because another package recommends or suggests it: only the first is in yapacc inspect orphans , and only the first would go with apt-get autoremove . Restart honours /run/reboot-required . On a Debian 13 machine, after the C library was reinstalled, it listed the same services as needrestart .

Both dnf 4 (Rocky 9, RHEL 9 family) and dnf5 (Fedora) are handled; their history output differs and both are parsed. Changes run dnf install , dnf remove and dnf upgrade --refresh . dnf can only simulate as root, so as an ordinary user the simulation runs through sudo ; in a run that may not ask for a password it runs behind sudo -n when that works, and is left out, with a line saying so, when it does not. The simulation ( --assumeno ) always ends with an error status, so yapacc reads dnf's messages, which it asks for in English ( LC_ALL=C ): a request dnf cannot resolve is refused before the gate. That includes the removal of a package dnf protects, such as sudo . Read commands never fetch. Left alone, dnf downloads repository metadata whenever its cache is stale, even for a query. yapacc asks it for cached data only ( -C ), and on a machine with no metadata on disk it says so and names dnf makecache instead of answering from nothing. Timeline reads dnf's own history database. Clean reports downloaded packages and repository metadata as two items, with dnf clean packages and dnf clean metadata . dnf5 also copies the repository metadata into ~/.cache/libdnf5 whenever an ordinary user asks it a question (84 MiB on a fresh Fedora 45), and check , search and briefing make it do so. yapacc cannot prevent that: pointed at the system cache, dnf5 fails for an ordinary user, because it writes there. clean lists the copy as an item of its own when it exists. Undo is dnf's own dnf history undo for the transaction shown, behind the gate. Before asking, yapacc checks that every old version is still in an enabled repository, because dnf would otherwise fail half-way through the question. There is no archive fallback: once the repository drops a version, that upgrade cannot be undone. Briefing takes security labels from dnf updateinfo . Restart uses needs-restarting -r for the reboot verdict.

Run undo and timeline with sudo . /var/log/zypp/history is readable by root only. openSUSE's sudo asks for the root password by default, and /usr/local/bin is not on its path, so install the binary into /usr/bin or give the full path. Changes run zypper install , zypper remove , and for an upgrade zypper dist-upgrade on Tumbleweed and zypper update on Leap. dnf installed beside zypper (openSUSE packages it) does not make the machine a dnf system: zypper stays the native manager, and yapacc platform lists dnf under other managers . Read commands never fetch. As root, zypper refreshes repositories on its own before answering. yapacc calls it for repository data only when every enabled repository has metadata on disk; otherwise it names the repositories that lack it and tells you to run zypper refresh . Why gives the repository that offers the package now. The zypp history does not record where the installed version came from, and the from line says so. Undo finds old versions in the repositories only. On Tumbleweed they are gone within a day or two of an upgrade; on Leap they stay longer. Kernels are multiversion packages: undoing a kernel upgrade removes the new kernel and leaves the old one, and is refused while the new kernel is the one running. Packages with no earlier record. libzypp writes an upgrade and a new install the same way. When undoing a whole upgrade, yapacc names the packages it cannot classify and asks at the terminal whether to remove them. --yes does not answer that question. Snapshots through snapper are the natural safety net here; see snapshots . Restart honours /run/reboot-needed .

Alpine uses doas , and yapacc uses it when there is no sudo . With opendoas, persist is tied to the calling process, so each yapacc run asks for the password once. Changes run apk add , apk del , and apk update then apk upgrade . Timeline reads /var/log/apk.log . Only apk-tools 3 writes that file, and only when run as root; on older Alpine releases there is no history, and timeline says so. No undo. yapacc does not reverse apk transactions. A run made with apk --quiet is logged without its package lines, so timeline cannot show what it changed. It counts those runs in a note. Use the static binary: Alpine is a musl system and the release archive is built for exactly that.

Changes run xbps-install , xbps-remove and xbps-install -Syu . No timeline and no undo. xbps keeps no log of transactions. doctor reports both as unavailable on Void, with that reason. Void's runit is detected; restart lists programs holding replaced files and tells you to restart services with sv restart NAME .

Build yapacc on FreeBSD itself; see install . Changes run pkg install , pkg delete and pkg upgrade . These cover packages, not the base system: freebsd-update and pkgbase upgrades of the base system remain yours to run. pkg install -n ends with an error status whenever there is something to install, so yapacc cannot judge the simulation by its status; it asks the catalogue on disk whether the name exists and refuses an unknown one before the gate, and it refuses when pkg itself says no package matches the name. Timeline reads the pkg lines in /var/log/messages . syslog stamps have no year and no zone; yapacc works the year out and keeps the time as written. Restart compares freebsd-version -k , -r and -u for the reboot verdict. Listing processes that hold replaced files needs the sysutils/checkrestart package. Snapshots on a ZFS root are taken with zfs snapshot of the root dataset. yapacc does not create boot environments; bectl is the tool for that. No undo. With no network, pkg itself can wait for minutes before giving up, and yapacc waits with it. The read commands answer from the catalogue on disk at once. sudo and doas both work. On FreeBSD doas with no terminal would wait forever for a password, so yapacc calls it non-interactively whenever nobody could type one.
Run yapacc platform and yapacc doctor . They do not guess: an unknown system gets "unknown" and the commands that cannot work there say so instead of trying.

yapacc --help lists the everyday commands. This page lists all of them, including the specialist ones it leaves out. yapacc help COMMAND prints the options of any command, and yapacc docs carries longer built-in topics. Commands marked read-only change nothing. Commands marked gated show a plan and stop at the gate .

Command What it answers why NAME Why is this package here? timeline What changed, and when? briefing What will the next upgrade do? clean What can be reclaimed? restart What must be restarted after an upgrade? configs Which configuration files are left unmerged? doctor What works on this machine? platform What kind of machine is this?
