On Arch, yapacc monitor check is a one-shot check for pending updates, meant for a timer, and yapacc monitor daemon-install installs a systemd timer that runs it (gated). Nothing of the kind is installed unless you run that command: see rule 2 in the introduction . On other systems both exit with code 6; use yapacc check from your own timer there.

Option Effect --json machine-readable output on read commands --script never prompt; fail fast --noconfirm consent in advance, like --yes on a gated command --config PATH use this configuration file -V , --version print the version Global options go before the command: yapacc --json why bash . Gated commands take --dryrun (plan only) and --yes (apply without asking) after the command: yapacc upgrade --dryrun .
yapacc needs no configuration. Without a file, the defaults below apply, and they are the safe ones: nothing is snapshotted or applied on its own.

~/.config/yapacc/config.toml , or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/yapacc/config.toml . Another path can be given for one run with --config PATH . An XDG_CONFIG_HOME that is empty or not an absolute path is ignored, as the XDG specification says, and the same holds for the cache, state and data directories: yapacc never derives one of its paths from the directory you happen to be in. prints the effective values and the file they were loaded from. yapacc never writes this file. A file that does not parse, or a known key with an invalid value, is an error (exit code 2). yapacc does not fall back to defaults silently, because a protective setting that quietly stops applying is worse than a command that refuses to run. A section or key it does not know gets one warning line each, and yapacc config lists them, so a typo such as [safty] does not go unnoticed. Paths in the file must be absolute or start with ~/ .
A complete example, yapacc.example.toml , ships with the source. The keys most people will want:
See snapshots .
See AI assistants .
For builds of third-party recipes (the AUR on Arch).

The ledger records what yapacc installed outside the native package manager (AppImages, flatpaks, isolated installs). Native packages are never recorded there; the package manager's own log is their record.

Variable Effect XDG_CONFIG_HOME , XDG_CACHE_HOME , XDG_STATE_HOME , XDG_DATA_HOME where the configuration, caches, the ledger and data live LC_ALL , LC_MESSAGES , LANG the letters of the [y/N] question NO_COLOR honoured by the interactive interface; the command line prints no colour codes

Option Effect --config PATH use this configuration file --json machine-readable output on the read commands; goes before the command --script never prompt; fail fast instead --noconfirm consent in advance, like --yes
yapacc is meant to be usable from scripts without parsing prose. Two things make that possible: read commands can print JSON, and the exit code says what kind of outcome it was.

Code Name Meaning 0 ok the command did what was asked 1 failed the operation ran and failed 2 usage bad arguments, or a configuration file that does not parse 3 refused a gate or a guard said no; nothing was changed 4 not found the package, record or plan does not exist 5 integrity a hash, signature or chain check failed 6 unavailable something the command needs is not available: a tool or an optional component that is not installed, a file this user may not read, a feature this build lacks, or a command that does not exist for this package manager The message goes to standard error as error: … . The codes that matter most in a script are 3 and 6. A 3 means the system is exactly as it was, by decision. A 6 means the machine lacks something, and the message names it.

--script promises that yapacc never prompts. A command that would have asked [y/N] is refused unless --yes or --dryrun is given, and a privilege tool that would have asked for a password is called in its non-interactive mode and fails at once. Without --script , yapacc still never reads an answer from a pipe: standard input that is not a terminal cannot confirm anything.

--json is a global option and goes before the command: These commands have a JSON form on every system: why , timeline , briefing , clean , restart , configs , doctor , platform , list , info , search , check , inspect owns , inspect files , inspect orphans , names , get --explain , snapshot list , config , capabilities , and the ledger reads. yapacc docs json prints the complete list, including the Arch-only ones. A command with no JSON form prints nothing and exits with code 2 ("no JSON output for this command"). It never prints prose with a success status, so a script cannot mistake one for the other. Fields are only ever added. Treat a key you do not know as ignorable, and do not depend on the order of keys. An empty answer is an empty array. In text mode the same answer is one line in parentheses, such as "(no orphan: every package installed as a dependency is still needed)", so that a blank screen never has to be interpreted. What a command has to add in words (a source it could not read, "no repository metadata on disk") goes to standard error as note: … lines. Standard output holds the JSON alone, so yapacc --json check | jq works on a machine that has never refreshed: the array is empty and the note says why. A few shapes that are useful to know: Command Shape platform one object; native_pkg_manager is "pacman" , "apt" , "dnf" , "zypper" , "apk" , "xbps" or "pkg" ; package_logs_unreadable lists the logs that exist and that this user may not read, and is left out when there is none why NAME one object; native.manager , native.reason , native.required_by[] , native.base , and orphan ( true , false or null ) timeline array of {ts, source, action, name, old_version, new_version} ; ts is Unix seconds doctor array of {name, state, detail} ; state is ok , warn , fail or n/a clean array of {what, size_bytes, count, safety, command, detail[]} list array of {name, version, description, …} check array of {name, old_version, new_version, repo} on every package manager; on apt repo holds every origin, separated by ", " ; on pacman it is "" for a repository update and "aur" for an AUR update The shapes of info and inspect orphans differ between pacman and the other package managers; yapacc docs json describes both.

h: A health check in two lines
t: The same list, filtered the other way: everything that is not ok on the machine of the quick start .
The release archive and the distribution packages install them for you.

yapacc i opens a full-screen interface in the terminal. It is an optional component, the separate program yapacc-tui ; when it is not installed, yapacc i says so and exits with code 6. It shows the same reports as the command line and adds nothing of its own. It is for exploring: reading the timeline, filtering the installed list, looking at what clean found.

The home screen is a menu of questions: what changed recently, what the next upgrade will do, what can be cleaned up, what works on this machine. Enter opens the highlighted line, and each line also has its own letter.

Where Key Action everywhere ? help Esc or q back; q on the home screen quits Ctrl-C quit at once j k , arrows, PgUp PgDn , g G move reports / filter by text r read again Enter show the whole line when it is cut u in the upgrade briefing: plan the upgrade o in the clean-up report: plan the removal of unneeded packages browsing Tab , 1 – 6 change tab Installed / filter, Space select, i why, d dependencies, x remove, e mark explicit Search type and Enter ; a install, i info, A include the AUR (Arch) External Enter details, x remove Run type any yapacc arguments; the output is shown, and nothing can prompt

h: Changing the system from the interface
t: The interface never answers a confirmation for you. Every change is first shown as a plan, which is a dry run: nothing has happened yet. To carry it out you move to [ Apply ] and press Enter . The interface then leaves the screen and runs the command in your terminal, where yapacc itself shows the plan and asks, exactly as described in the gate . The sudo or doas password prompt appears there as well. Run the interface as yourself. There is no reason to start it as root. The Run tab shows output only. It does not run a command with --yes or --noconfirm , because nothing typed there has been through the plan screen. Without a terminal, yapacc i exits with code 6.

yapacc mcp runs a server that speaks the Model Context Protocol over standard input and output. An AI assistant that supports MCP can connect to it and use yapacc as a set of tools: ask why a package is installed, read the timeline, get the upgrade briefing, and propose a change. It is an optional component, the separate program yapacc-mcp . yapacc contains no AI and holds no API key. The assistant, the model and the billing are whatever you already use; yapacc is only the tool it calls.

h: What an assistant can and cannot do
t: By default an assistant can read and propose . It cannot apply. When it asks for an install, a removal, an upgrade or an undo, the server returns the plan and the exact command for you to run in your own terminal, where the gate asks you. The tool's answer tells the assistant not to claim that anything was changed. This does not depend on the assistant behaving well. The tools accept a confirm argument, and an assistant can set it to true and say you approved. It makes no difference: unless the machine's administrator has said otherwise, the server never applies.

Two things are needed, and both must be true: apply = "allow" under [mcp] in a configuration file that is owned by root and not writable by anyone else , passed to the server with --config ; the assistant sets confirm to true on the call. The file has to be root's because your own configuration file is something an assistant with access to your files could edit. apply = "allow" in a file you own is ignored: the server prints a warning when it starts and stays in plan mode. apply = "allow" means you trust the assistant's statement that you approved. Privileges still apply: a change needs sudo or doas , and with no terminal those are called in non-interactive mode, so it works only where passwordless privileges exist for that command. Think before combining the two. Nothing records that a change was requested by an assistant: the native log shows it like any other.
Point your assistant's MCP configuration at the command yapacc mcp . For clients that use a JSON configuration: The server speaks protocol revision 2024-11-05.

Read-only tools, which change nothing: Tool What it returns yapacc_platform the kind of machine: distribution, package manager, init, snapshots yapacc_doctor what works on this machine yapacc_why why a package is installed yapacc_timeline package changes, newest first yapacc_briefing what the next upgrade will do yapacc_check pending updates yapacc_clean_report what can be reclaimed yapacc_restart_report what must be restarted after an upgrade yapacc_pending_configs configuration files left unmerged yapacc_snapshots existing filesystem snapshots yapacc_search , yapacc_resolve , yapacc_plan find a package, choose a source, show the install plan yapacc_names what a package is called on other distributions yapacc_ledger , yapacc_capabilities , yapacc_news installs outside the package manager; host capabilities; Arch news Staged tools. The answer of each begins with one of these lines, so that neither you nor the assistant has to guess what happened: The answer begins with Meaning PLAN ONLY — nothing was changed. the plan, and the command for you to run in your own terminal PLAN ONLY (confirm=false) — nothing was changed. applying is allowed, and the call did not say confirm: true PLAN FAILED — nothing was changed. the plan could not be made: a package no source has, a package to remove that is not installed, a failed simulation APPLIED: … the change was made; only when applying is allowed FAILED: … the change was tried and failed Tool Proposes yapacc_install installing a package yapacc_remove removing native packages yapacc_upgrade a full system upgrade yapacc_undo_last taking the last transaction back

The server itself opens no socket and listens on nothing. Some tools make yapacc contact a server, exactly as the matching command does: see safety and privacy . yapacc_names sends the package name to repology.org, and its description tells the assistant so.
What yapacc protects you from, what it does not, what it sends over the network and what it writes to disk. The design reasoning behind this page is in SECURITY.md .

Changing the system without your say. Every change goes through the gate . Without --yes it asks; with nobody to ask it refuses. An AI assistant connected through MCP cannot apply anything unless you enabled that in the configuration. Surprises in what is run. The plan, the native manager's own simulation of it, and the exact command are printed before the question. Names that are not names. Package names are validated against the character set a package name can have, and passed to the native manager as separate arguments after -- . No shell command line is ever built from package data, log contents or network answers. Half-applied undos. undo is all or nothing. If one old version cannot be found, or one download fails its check, nothing is changed. Removing the ground you stand on. An undo that would remove the running kernel is refused. Hostile build recipes (the AUR on Arch). The PKGBUILD is shown for review before anything is built. The build then runs in a bubblewrap sandbox: your home directory and /run are hidden, the environment is cleared, and the network is available only while sources are downloaded. Terminal tricks. Escape sequences in package names, file names and log lines are neutralised before they are printed.

h: What it does not protect against
t: A package you agreed to install. Once you answer yes, the native package manager runs as root and package scripts do what they do. yapacc is not a sandbox for native packages. Lost configuration or data. undo restores package versions only. If an upgrade rewrote a configuration file or migrated a database, undo does not bring the old one back. A snapshot does. A compromised repository. yapacc relies on your package manager's signature checks and adds none of its own for native packages. Weakly verified archive downloads. When undo has to fetch an old version from an archive, the verification depends on the archive. A package from the Arch Linux Archive must carry a signature that verifies, or the undo stops. A file from snapshot.debian.org is compared with the hash the service records, which is not a signature. Launchpad downloads are not verified. The plan says which case applies to each package before you are asked. A determined build. The build sandbox has no seccomp filter and no resource limits. It keeps a recipe away from your files; it is not a virtual machine. A local attacker who is already you. The configuration file and the ledger of non-native installs live in your home directory. Something running as you can change them.

Some of what yapacc prints is other people's text. Answers from the AUR and from Repology, and the names of systemd units, are printed with control characters replaced or escaped, so that a crafted name cannot move the cursor, recolour the screen or hide a line. Package names are validated before they are used in a plan.

yapacc has no telemetry, no update check of its own and no listening socket. These are the only cases in which it contacts a server: Command Contacts What is sent names NAME repology.org the package name undo the distribution's archive: archive.archlinux.org, snapshot.debian.org or launchpad.net the name and version of each package it needs briefing the distribution's news feed, where there is one (Arch); skipped with --offline nothing but the request check , get , and the AUR commands, on Arch aur.archlinux.org the names of packages that are not in the repositories; the name you ask for install , remove , upgrade , refresh your repositories, through your package manager whatever your package manager sends anything you give a URL to that URL Every other read command works offline, from what is on disk. On a machine with no network at all, why , timeline , clean , restart , configs , doctor , platform , list , info , search and check answer as usual.

Read commands write nothing. The complete list of places yapacc writes to: Path When ~/.cache/yapacc/ old packages while an undo runs (deleted when it ends); build caches and the throwaway home of a sandboxed build ~/.local/state/yapacc/ledger/ (or /var/lib/yapacc/ledger/ as root) when you install something outside the package manager through yapacc ~/.local/share/yapacc/ , ~/Applications/yapacc/ AppImages, isolated installs and recipes, if you use those commands ./NAME-aur-build in the current directory install aur NAME (Arch) a file you name plan … --out FILE , index build --path FILE and similar systemd timer units only if you run monitor daemon-install It never writes its configuration file, never edits your shell startup files, and never adds a hook to your package manager.
Please report security problems privately, as described in SECURITY.md at the top of the repository , and not in a public issue.

h: Do I have to stop using apt, pacman or dnf?
t: No. Keep using them. yapacc reads what they record and is never confused by a change you made directly. Its own install , remove and upgrade are a convenience with a uniform gate, not a requirement.

h: Does it keep its own database of my packages?
t: No. Every answer is read from the package manager at the moment you ask. The only thing yapacc records is what it installed outside the package manager (an AppImage, an isolated install), because nothing else would remember those.

h: Does anything run in the background?
t: No. There is no daemon, no timer and no package-manager hook. A timer for update checks exists as an option you have to install yourself with yapacc monitor daemon-install .

It changes packages, so it deserves the same care as any downgrade. It is built to refuse when it cannot do the whole job: it will not apply half an undo, will not remove the running kernel, and shows the native manager's own simulation before asking. What it cannot do is restore configuration or data that the upgrade changed. For that, take a snapshot before big upgrades.

h: How far back can I undo?
t: One transaction: the last one. And only if the old versions can still be found. On pacman, apt on Debian and apt on Ubuntu there is a distribution archive to fall back on. On dnf and zypper there is not.

h: Why is there no curl | sh installer?
t: Because the point of the tool is that you see what will happen first. The install page is six lines, and you can read every one.

h: Is it safe to give an AI assistant access?
t: In the default configuration the assistant can read and propose, and cannot apply. See AI assistants for what changes if you allow more.

h: What does "tier 1" in yapacc platform mean?
t: It is the support level of your package manager; see what works where .
It is the licence the author chose. yapacc runs your package manager as a separate program and links none of its code.

h: error: … is not on PATH (exit code 6)
t: A tool that command needs is missing, and the message names it. Common ones: curl (for names , the news feed and undo downloads), sudo or doas (for any change as an ordinary user). sudo yapacc … cannot find the binary on openSUSE when it is installed in /usr/local/bin : openSUSE's sudo does not search there. Use the full path or install into /usr/bin .

h: timeline or undo says it cannot read the log
t: Some distributions keep the package log readable by root only (openSUSE's /var/log/zypp/history ). Run the command with sudo .

On Void: xbps keeps no log, so there is nothing to show. On Alpine: /var/log/apk.log is written by apk-tools 3 only. After a log rotation: rotated and compressed logs are read, but a distribution that deletes old logs deletes that history.

h: undo is refused: "in no cache, repository or archive"
t: The exact old version of some package can no longer be found. On rolling distributions without an archive (Tumbleweed) this happens a day or two after an upgrade. A filesystem snapshot is the remedy next time; there is no remedy afterwards.

h: --script fails with "Authorization required" or "a password is required"
t: --script never prompts, so sudo or doas is called in its non-interactive mode. Either run as root, or allow that one command without a password in sudoers or doas.conf . yapacc tells you whether the tool refused for lack of a password or for lack of a rule.

h: The command stopped with exit code 3
t: That is a refusal, and nothing was changed. Either you answered no, or the command could not ask ( --script , a pipe, no terminal) and you gave neither --yes nor --dryrun . See the gate .
It depends on the system having a source for that: the security repository on Debian and Ubuntu, advisory data on dnf and zypper, arch-audit on Arch. Where there is none, a note: line says so.

h: restart lists nothing, but I just upgraded
t: As an ordinary user you can only examine your own processes. The last lines say how many could not be examined. Run it with sudo .

h: The [y/N] question is in another language
t: It follows your locale ( LC_MESSAGES ). English y and yes are accepted in every locale.

Open an issue at github.com/ezechiel203/yapacc with the output of these two commands and the exact command that misbehaved: yapacc timeline --html > timeline.html adds the recent package history as one self-contained file, if the problem appeared after an upgrade. Look through it first: it lists your installed package names. For a security problem, do not open a public issue. See safety and privacy .
